utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. May I begin by calling for the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm Tom Hannis with case manager Crispian Smith for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Cvijetic, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, and Tatjana Savic representing the Defence of Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Karim Khan, duty counsel for Mr. Zupljanin; accompanied by the permanent and regular case manager for the accused, Mr. Eric Tully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. The Chamber takes note of the fact that the accused Stojan Zupljanin has chosen to the absent from the proceedings this morning. I have not been informed of the reasons why Mr. Zupljanin is absent, but the Chamber was advised last night when we adjourned that he might not wish to attend the proceedings in the absence of his appointed counsel. The Chamber has considered the matter, and we have come to the conclusion that we shall, nevertheless, proceed with the next witness, witness ST-177. Sorry, ST-196. And the reasons why the Chamber has so decided are the following: First of all, we assume that the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination of the witness today will not be concluded by the end of the proceedings today, and will, therefore, continue tomorrow, at which point we assume that counsel will be back in his seat and that Stojan Zupljanin also will attend the proceedings. So there will be ample options for counsel tomorrow to cross-examine the witness. For the purpose of allowing Defence counsel to be fully appraised of the proceedings during this day, the Chamber orders the Registrar to make available to Defence counsel video recordings of the proceedings this morning so as to enable the appointed counsel to familiarise himself with what has transpired from the proceedings today before counsel resumes his seat tomorrow. And since Mr. Zupljanin anyway is represented today by duty counsel who will be able to take care of his interests to the best of his ability, we have concluded that there is no prejudice made to Mr. Zupljanin by continuing to hear the next witness and so we kindly ask the Registrar to bring in the next witness. The Chamber also takes notice of the fact that counsel for Mr. Zupljanin announced last week that he -- or rather, that the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin probably would not have questions for cross-examination to this witness exceeding 15 minutes, and we will in addition also enable Defence counsel tomorrow when we resume the proceedings to address any issue arising out of the proceedings today before we continue tomorrow. So with these precautions, the Chamber believes that we have taken every possible step to safe-guard the interests of Mr. Zupljanin and so we think we can proceed from here. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the record and for the benefit of duty counsel, Mr. Khan, I would indicate this witness was a policeman in Zvornik. His testimony relates entirely to Zvornik, he makes no mention of Mr. Zupljanin, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Banja Luka, or anything of that. So I would be surprised if there was anything that arose that would be pertaining to Mr. Zupljanin, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honours, I can confirm, in fact, on the information provided by Mr. Tully, who, of course, is a regular part of Defence team, that in fact it is not anticipated that there will be any question whatsoever for this witness. The 15 minutes that was indicated, I'm told, was simply a reservoir that could be dipped into if unexpected matters arose in the course of questioning. But it's anticipated there's no questions at all for the witness that will be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Madam Registrar, let's have the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, next witness then is Petko Panic. ST-196. He has no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Could you begin by telling us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I am Petko Panic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your date of birth is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 28th of July, 1952.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your occupation or profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently retired. I used to work in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you given evidence before either at the Tribunal or within the region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not here, but I did testify in Belgrade in the proceedings against Ranko Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been called by the Prosecution in this matter and what will happen is that the side calling you, in this case the Prosecution, will first lead you in your testimony. And then there will be an opportunity for counsel representing the accused to cross-examine you, if they wish. Then may follow re-examination by the Prosecution, after which the Bench may have some questions of you. So before I invite the counsel for the Prosecution to begin, do you have any questions in terms of what I would have explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Panic. You told us that you are retired from the MUP. Can you tell us when you began your police career and for how long you worked as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I started on the 1st of September, 1973. And I worked until I retired on the 31st of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during that time where did you work as a policeman? What municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: The entire time in Zvornik municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the highest rank you achieved before retiring?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: In 1995 -- in late 1994 I was appointed commander, which is to say that throughout 1995 and until March of 1996 I was a commander of a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as commander of the police station, I take it that was in the Zvornik. How many men worked under you, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly because up until the signing of the Dayton Agreement, we still had some reserve forces members, and I would say that there were about 100 members of the general police at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in 1991 and early 1992 before the conflict began in Bosnia, what was your job at the Zvornik police station?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Just before the war I was head of the patrol sector. I and my assistant were in charge of the patrol sector covering two or three local communes. And then in September 1991 reserve police stations -- or, rather, reserve police war station were mobilised, and I was assistant commander for the reserve police station in Zvornik. Up until the conflict broke out, both Muslim and Serb policemen served there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before the conflict broke out, it's my understanding Zvornik municipality was a multi-ethnic community. Can you tell us approximately what the percentages were of Muslims, Serbs, and others?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was multi-ethnic. About 64 per cent of the population and the town of Zvornik were Muslims, and the remaining were Serbs. And as for the entire municipality it was approximately 50/50 because the neighbouring villages were mostly Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about within the police force itself, what was the split? Did it reflect the same percentage roughly that existed in the general population?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think so. I don't remember the exact figures, but when it comes to the general police station without traffic police there were about 24 to 25 policemen of Serb ethnicity, and 30 or so were Muslims. This was just before the war broke out, so it was about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of a document that was sent out by Momcilo Mandic on or about the 31st of March, 1992, calling for the Serb police to separate?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I personally did not see that document, but at the Secretariat of the Interior it was discussed that the Assembly had adopted such a decision and that a letter had arrived. A letter to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened when you first became aware of that? What happened with you and the other Serb policemen in Zvornik SJB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Well, all the way up until the 6th of April we continued working together, and prior to that letter of the 6th of April, there was an attack against the army at a place called Sapna and a warrant officer was killed there. And then on the 29th of March, deputy commander of the traffic police mobilised during the night, policemen of Muslim origin, to secure the Secretariat of the Interior. And then on the following day an inspector came from Tuzla, they had a discussion, and after that we continued working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For how much longer did you continue working together?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Up until the 6th of April in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened then to change things?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, I was at work in the evening and then assistant commander Eric, Slavko came to me, he had been to see other policemen who were working, and then came to me and said that commander -- I don't know if he is protected, but commander Dragan Spasojevic had ordered that all Serb policemen withdraw to Karakaj with all of the vehicles that they were using and all materiel and equipment and that they should take all of that to Alhos in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is Karakaj and where is it in relation to Zvornik town?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Karakaj is an industrial settlement 3 and a half kilometres from Zvornik in the direction of Bijeljina at the intersection of the road leading to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was Alhos? What was Alhos?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Alhos was a textile manufacturing factory before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did you and the other Serb policemen then do what Slavko Eric had directed you to do and go to Alhos with the equipment and vehicles you could find?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, and there we found commander Spasojevic, president of the municipality Brano Grujic, and we also found there some Arkan's men, Seselj's men, which we didn't know at the time, we learned of this later. And we were given an assignment to set up check-points. I was with a group at a check-point for Mali Zvornik, and then there was a check-point at the intersection for Tuzla, at the intersection for Sapna, and later on a check-point was set up at the entry point in Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the last check-point?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Intersection for Sapna and then Vidakova Njiva is a settlement at the entry point in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Brano Grujic was there at Alhos as well. Were there any other political authorities or political body that went to Alhos at the same time you police went there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that most of them were from the then Crisis Staff, Jovo Mijatovic, Jovan Ivanovic. They kept coming and going. Mitrovic, and the rest, they were coming and going. I'm not sure about the times, but I used to see all of them there. Cedo. Stevo Radic, not Cedo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any other members of the Zvornik Crisis Staff in addition to Brano Grujic, Jovo Mijatovic, Stevo Radic, and Mr. Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Jovo Ivanovic was a member. In addition to Mijatovic, there is also Jovo Ivanovic. I think that Mile Mijic was the then chief of the Serb police. And then Vinko Radic, and I really couldn't remember the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. You mentioned Mile Milic -- Mile Mijic as the then chief of the Serb police. When did he become chief of the Serb police, and who put him in that position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that he was appointed chief immediately after the 31st of March, and the meeting that was held in Zvornik municipality, the meeting of the SDS, that he was then appointed chief of the Serb police, and Dragan Spasojevic was appointed commander. And Dragan Spasojevic had already been commander of this police station, so then when the split occurred, the posts were -- because Osman Mustafic used to be chief and Dragan Spasojevic commander. And then Mile Mijic was appointed to his position, and Dragan remained serving as commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed Mijic to that position?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that at that time it was the political party that appointed him. I don't know whether the MUP was informed of that, but I think that it was the SDS party that appointed them, or the Crisis Staff, whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what had Mr. Mijic done before he was put in that position? Was he a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, he was a judge at the municipal court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long he remained as the chief of the Zvornik Serb police?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: For a month, month and a half at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us who replaced him. Who was the next chief?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milos Pantelic came to replace him. He was from Loznica, he used to be commander of traffic police in Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When Milos Pantelic took up that position, who was selected as commander of the police, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Dragan Spasojevic remained there for awhile and then he left, but then after Dragan Spasojevic went to a company called Autotransport, he was replaced by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the person who replaced Dragan Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Marinko Vasilic [realtime transcript read in error "Vasiljevic"].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know there were several changes in the position. Who -- well, do you recall approximately how long Milos Pantelic remained as chief before he was replaced?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: A correction. I see something on the screen. It says Marinko Vasiljevic, and it should be Marinko Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for catching that, I didn't notice.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milos Pantelic remained until June. Until mid-June, perhaps. I know that when we went to Belgrade somebody used to show a document that was signed by Milos Pantelic on the 6th of June, so perhaps sometime around the 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we later will see a document on or about the 9th of June where there is a different person who is listed as the chief. Who was the person who followed Milos Pantelic as chief of Zvornik SJB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: After Milos Pantelic, Marinko Vasilic who used to be commander became chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when Marinko Vasilic moved up to become chief, who became the new commander?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Momcilo Maric. My name was also proposed, but since Momcilo Maric was a senior policeman and he had higher educational qualification than I did, he was appointed and not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more, I think. After -- how long did Marinko Vasilic remain in the position of chief? Until when approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Officially until the 27th of June when we expelled Gogic's men, and he remained officially for a day or two. He was put on the waiting list, and then the other person came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your answer is translated as the 27th of June. But I believe from other documents it was July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: July, July. July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the name of the person who replaced Mr. Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milorad Lokanjcevic, also known as Mico Lokanjcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was he? Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Before the war he used to work in the MUP of Kalesija municipality. And then from the MUP he was appointed chief and Branislav Mihajlovic was appointed commander; he was from Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, and Lokanjcevic remained as chief throughout the rest of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document this is 65 ter 3024. It will come up on the screen in front of you in a second, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 6th of April, 1992. I don't know if the page numbers are in the correct order. I think it's on the right-hand side of the e-court page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Let me just see if I can read this. Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's entitled: A decision on the declaration of state of war on the territory of Zvornik municipality, issued by the Crisis Staff. Were you aware that such a decision had taken place on or about the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't involved in this. I didn't see this, but I didn't know -- but I did learn about this later from the discussions I had, that there had been a decision on declaring the state of war. But since I wasn't involved in had the work of the Crisis Staff, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Article number 4 in the document indicates that the defence duties will be taken over by the Territorial Defence and some parts of the reserve police. Did that actually take place, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This is not clear to me. In what sense, defence? At that time in Zvornik itself, there were no war operations, but there were check-points. Now, if the TO asked for a certain number of policemen to be sent to the front line, then, yes, they were sent them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you can see item number 6, it indicates that the decision enters into force on the date of adoption and was to be announced on the radio stations Podrinje in Loznica and Zvornik radio. Did you hear any announcements or were you listening to the radio at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't have much time to follow the radio, but there probably was such announcement. The police did secure the building of the radio station. Most likely this was announced on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 3024.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you, the police and Mr. Grujic and others had moved out to Alhos on about the 6th of April. What happened there during the next day or two? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: During that period of time we just performed our regular police duties. We manned check-points, we inspected people and vehicles passing through. And then on the 7th it was announced that they should enter Zvornik, that Arkan's unit would prepare the entry into Zvornik and that 50 to 100 people should escort him to secure certain facilities, to provide security to certain facilities. This is what was discussed. One of Arkan's men was called Pejic, and it was discussed with him. Once I saw Arkan and Brano in front of the Crisis Staff discussing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A few questions from your last answer. Mr. Pejic with Arkan's men, did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: He used to be called Pejo. He had a Serbian uniform, a blue camouflage uniform, and he had a rank. I think he was the general or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said you saw Arkan and Brano in front of the Crisis Staff. Brano, do you mean Mr. Grujic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Grujic. On the 7th they held a meeting in the Jezero hotel in Mali Zvornik which was also attended by the president of the Muslim municipality of Zvornik, and they attempted to try to agree how to divide the municipality starting from the river Zlatica toward Karakaj, to remain Serbian, and the rest would be Muslim. And that initially they would start with joint patrols; however, later when Dragan Spasojevic and Brano returned, we heard that Sanov [as interpreted] slapped all of them including the Muslim representative, and he said there would be no agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It looks like on the transcript the interpreters didn't catch the name of the person you said slapped all of them and said there would be no agreement. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, on the 7th of April, there was some sort of meeting held in Mali Zvornik, which on the Serb -- in Serbia, where political representatives of both the Muslim and Serb side were discussing the possibility of dividing up the municipality in some fashion?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Or how to make arrangements about joint patrol which would be doing the work pending the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Arkan apparently was the person or the reason that no such agreement was reached because he slapped the people who were even discussing it?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, he beat them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did you know who Arkan was before you saw him in Alhos on or about the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: All I knew about him was what I saw on TV before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when had you seen him on TV before?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: There were discussions about his being the leader of supporters of the football club Red Star, how he had gone to Croatia during the war, and such-like things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you seen or heard anything about him in relation to a Serb take-over in Bijeljina a week or a few days before?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I also heard about that on TV, that it was captured by Arkan's men. I didn't see him. I only saw Mirko Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The Arkan's men that were in Alhos on the 6th of April, how were they dressed and equipped?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms, but those uniforms were much more modern than ours. They had automatic weapons, Scorpions. Some of those weapons I had never even seen before, although I was working for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many Arkan's men, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It depended. There were different numbers at different times. They were billeted at Banja Radaljska and came over as necessary and if necessary, sometimes 5 of them, 10, or 30 of them. All of that was in the vicinity, and they had vehicles that would drive them from Radaljska Banja quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned as well Seselj's men. How were they dressed and equipped?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Most of them were dressed in olive drab camouflage uniforms. And they had automatic weapons, they had knives, they had cockades on their caps, the Serbian cockades, they also had some patches on their sleeves, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Earlier you told me it was decided that Arkan's would lead the way into Zvornik town. Do you know how it was decided or by whom it was decided that would occur?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I think that that was decided between their leadership and the Crisis Staff. This was done at some higher level into which I had no insight. All I know is that we were ordered to board the buses and follow Arkan's men. And I also think that the TO company joined us, so at the entrance to Zvornik we stopped and somebody said two or three policemen and three or four military men are going to secure this building, then we went to the municipal building. Then we went to hospital to secure all those facilities. And also we manned check-point at the exit point from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said that you -- or you said: "We were ordered to board the buses and follow Arkan's men." Who ordered you to do that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Station commander. And I probably -- he received his order from the chief because the chief was the one who attended the meetings at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the commander on that day was Dragan Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened when you all got into Zvornik that day? And first of all, tell me which day was this that Arkan's and the rest of you entered Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 8th of April upon our entry into Zvornik, but I saw in my previous statement that there was a mistake. It says technical school centre, but it should be secondary technical centre. Anyway, I saw three bodies, and then further on I saw one or two bodies. And later on I heard that it was confirmed that two bodies had been found there. I disembarked from the bus near the Radio Zvornik building, and I stayed there to secure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on what you saw and heard, was there any serious resistance by the Muslims to the entry into Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. When they heard that Arkan's men and Seselj's men were coming, they were already leaving the town and heading towards Kula Grad, so there were only a few people left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The bodies you say you saw, can you tell us any more about them? How they were dressed, whether you could see any wounds on them, whether or not they had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, we just passed by in the bus. They were on the pavement there. Later on I found out that Nale [phoen] Fahrudin was the one who -- one of them, and that he had been working at the staff before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what clothes were these bodies wearing? Uniforms? Civilian?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: All those who were by the school were dressed in civilian clothes, blue jeans, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now what did you and the other policemen do after Arkan's and the Seselj's men entered Zvornik and obtained control of some of the major buildings?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: We were instructed to secure vital facilities and to patrol the town. But whenever we went on patrol, there was always one or two Arkan's men with us. We were not able to enter the SUP building because it was already devastated. After Arkan's men entered the SUP, they took away all the documents, all the equipment, and everything was broken and destroyed; therefore, we stayed at the hotel. But that happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you remain in Zvornik securing buildings and patrolling?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that on the first or the second night we heard that Arkan's men fled or withdrew to Radaljska Banja without any agreement with the staff, and that Seselj men did the same, meaning that we were the only ones who remained in town. Then we withdrew as well, and we went to Alhos. We crossed the bridge to Mali Zvornik, and then we went on to Alhos in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did you stay at Alhos? How many days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Not long. When we arrived in Alhos, we started again wearing our JNA caps with a five-pointed star. Then a man from Seselj's unit came and he started beating one of our fellow police officers saying, Why do you need these stars for. Then Milos Milanovic, a policeman, pointed a gun at him and chased him out. We got dressed, and we went to the village of Celopek to a football playground near the house of Slavko Eric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your purpose for going to Celopek?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: We felt safer there because there were neither Muslims nor paramilitary forces there. We went there to see how to proceed, and we agreed eventually that we should all go home. Those who lived further than Kozluk were afraid to going through Kozluk, and, therefore, we were thinking of going through Mali Zvornik and Loznica. However, after some time, President Brano Grujic came, and after talking to him, we agreed to go back to Zvornik again, and that is what we did. Dragan and Brana and maybe somebody else went to Radaljska Banja and reached an agreement for Arkan's men to return as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go then, into Zvornik, into the old SJB building, or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: We would only come to provide security, but we billeted in Karakaj. Whether it was in the standard building or some place else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us about the Alhos building before. What was the Standard building? What was Standard?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: That was a newly constructed building for the Standard company, but they never moved in. Later it was used by the army as its barracks, and nowadays it houses a university department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And both of those buildings are in the Karakaj area. Are they -- can you tell us where they were approximately vis-a-vis the Karakaj Technical School?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Alhos is situated on the left-hand side if you watch -- if you look downstream the Drina, opposite Zvornik and Bijeljina on the right-hand side. And the Standard is also on the right-hand side near Zvornik in the direction of Bijeljina, by the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And their position as relates to the Karakaj Technical School, how far away?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies let's say some 50 metres between Alhos and technical school. And as for Standard, I should say about 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you another document from April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 3084. And ask what you know about this one. It will be up on the screen in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's entitled: A decision by the interim government of Zvornik, signed by President Grujic. It's entitled: "To give authority to the Loznica and Mali Zvornik police stations to take civilians into custody and hand them over to the Zvornik SJB." Did you ever see that document before?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't, but I knew of it. And I know that people had been brought into the Mali Zvornik station and taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions about it. Mali Zvornik and Loznica were in Serbia, in the Republic of Serbia, not in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you help me out, legally how was President Grujic of the interim government of Zvornik in Bosnia able to give authority to police in Serbia to do anything?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't think that he gave direct authorities to the police. He rather agreed with the presidents of those municipalities. Because at the time it was considered still to be Yugoslavia. So I don't know exactly what the legal basis was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I right, is the purpose of this to get military-aged Serbs who may have gone across the river back into Bosnia and have them help you out?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in order for them to join the military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us you were aware of this and that you know that that did happen sometimes, that some local Bosnian Serbs who had gone across the river were actually arrested and brought back to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once a full bus was brought from Serbia and they were immediately deployed on the front line whether in Trnovo or in Bandjerka or some place else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I would tender 3084 a this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I would like to show you an exhibit that's already in evidence. This is P141.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document from the Bijeljina CSB chief Predrag Jesuric, dated the 21st of April, 1992. And I just want to ask your comment about an entry on the first page, if we can go down near the bottom, there's a heading Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, I guess in the Serbian we have to go to page 2 at the top. Page 2 of the text, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see at the top there, it says, "Zvornik SJB Chief Mijic reported over the phone" -- it says "... the town is under Serbian militia and reserve TO control, and the town is building cleaned." Is that consistent with the situation on 21st April 1992, as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think yes, because as I said even when we were entering Zvornik, there was no resistance, and then later on there was no fighting in town itself. As far as the police was concerned, they started doing their regular duties of securing facilities. All these paramilitary units and army units were separate from each other, and they were mostly deployed in the suburbs of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to have you look at 65 ter number 2121. With the usher's help I can hand you a hard copy, that way we won't have to turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, this purports to be a list of active policemen in the Zvornik police station, dated 21 April 1992. I think you saw this during proofing. Do you recognise the names on that list?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you pointed out a couple of things regarding the translation. Number 4 Miljanovic, the English translation says deputy commander, but I think you told me it should be something else.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, number 4 is Miljanovic, assistant commander; and number 2, Petko Panic, deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And for numbers 8 through 15, there's an abbreviation VPS is the English translation, and it's suggested that meant military police station, but I think you told me VPS stands for something else. Could you tell us what that was.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, VPS stands for the patrol sector leader within a police station. They each cover three or four local communes, and this leader would have one or two assistants. So these are the titles in the police, not the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with those corrections noted, I would tender 2121. I can submit this for CLSS to have a corrected translation, but I think the record read together with the document accurately reflects it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P325, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally before you take it away, could you see the signature or the name on the last page? Who was the chief at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milos Pantelic, the chief. But there's no signature and there's no stamp either. And he says here that I was deputy commander, whereas at the time I was assistant commander. Maybe I stood in for Maric unofficially, but officially I was not his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you a related document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 2113. 65 ter 2113. [Microphone not activated] Sorry, Your Honours, I've got to correct the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These are some payroll sheets from Zvornik, and I'm trying to find the one that pertains to you and the other police.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It was on the monitor before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Witness. Let me return to that one after the break. And I'll move to something else for the moment. Now, in addition to the police, you've told us about there was a Crisis Staff and told us who some of the members were. What other organisations were in Zvornik at the time on the Serb side? What about the Territorial Defence, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: There was the People's Defence Staff and an army brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall who was head of the Territorial Defence staff in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: At the time he was known to us as Marko Pavlovic and later on during the trial in Belgrade, I learned that his name was Branko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was he, where was he from, how did he come to be in Zvornik in the Territorial Defence, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: How he came there, I don't know, but I do know that he came from Serbia. Now, who had brought him there, I don't know. People were saying that he was from Novi Sad or from Zrenjanin, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how this man who came from Serbia got to be at the head of the Territorial Defence in Zvornik? Who put him in that position, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Most likely civilian authorities from Zvornik because no ordinary person could have appointed him or invited him to come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the army, the JNA had been the Army of Yugoslavia that was -- or the People's Army, but what happened after the split and the conflict began, were there any elements of the army that were working with you on the Serb side in April and May before the VRS was created?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Various groups came from Serbia. A group with Zuca Vuckovic. Then there was a group that came with Niski, so-called Niski. And then there was the Pivarski group. Then there was Simo Chetnik. There were White Eagles who held Snagovo. So there were a lot of these paramilitary units in Zvornik. Later on some of them joined the TO and some joined the army, but for the most part they worked on their own, independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after mid-May when the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army was created, were there elements of that in Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was, but I don't remember whether it was a brigade or some other unit, but their commander was Colonel Vasilic and later on Colonel Blagojevic. And at one point in time Zuca took over by force so that he was a brigade commander for awhile, and he was busy constructing an armoured train, just didn't have a chance to complete it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Colonel Vasilic, is that the same last name as one of your SJB chiefs?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Same last name but not the same person. I don't know his first name. But he had been an officer back in the Army of Yugoslavia, as was Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to mention some other names of army officers and ask you if they were in the Zvornik municipality during May, June, July of 1992. How about a Colonel Ilic? I think his first name was Dragutin?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I didn't see him, so I don't remember him. I think that there was Dragan Obrenovic there, he used to be there previously too. He had his own unit there as did Mirko Studeni who was a captain at the time. They used to train reserve forces at Vranje and Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about a man named Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: He came later on after the establishment. Dragan and Studeni had been there earlier before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this is an appropriate time for our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll be trying to use 65 ter 2113 again, and I think I need page 2 of the B/C/S to correspond with page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It was the one, wasn't it, where the witness's name appeared?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, I'm going to try again with those pay sheets. I think I've got the right page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could shrink the B/C/S page down so we can see across the width of the page and be sure to include the first five names on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 21st of August and purports to be the list for payments of salaries for July 1992 for the public security station in Zvornik. You recognise that document, and the names on the list?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it that is you at number 3? And that was your salary in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A series of names here, I think that goes to a total of about 200. Is that consistent with the number of people who were working and being paid by the police in Zvornik in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: At that time most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 2113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To show what, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to show who were working for the police and being paid by the police. I have another document I am going to show relating to salaries being paid to other persons. It, I think, is important to identify who was working for which organ and being paid by which organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P326, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next could we look at 65 ter number 1391.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Panic, you'll recall your salary that we just looked at I think was 18.000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This next one is document regarding salaries for the TO for the month of May 1992. Do you recognise any of the names on that list?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I recognise a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Pavlovic, Marko; Sekanic, Aco; Tomic, Milos; Petkovic, Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we see that the salary for the month of May for Marko Pavlovic was 130.000 dinars. The document also lists number of days in combat. Were you aware of the TO and these individuals being involved in combat operations during the month of May in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is right. Most of these people were at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at page 3 of the English, and I think it's page 3 of the B/C/S as well. If we can have the entire list shown on the screen for the witness. And English on the right-hand side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Again, this is a list of members of the TO staff including some support personnel, I would say, typist, cleaning, coffee lady. And it appears that coffee lady is being paid 60.000 dinars, more than three times the amount you were paid as an assistant commander for the police. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know what their salaries were, but I can see that it was much higher than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to the war, just as a matter of curiosity, do you know what the pay levels were in the Territorial Defence versus pay levels in the police? Or did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: They were always lower. It depends on the post, of course, but if it was the same educational background, then lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was lower, police was lower than the TO or vice-versa?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: TO, because we had accelerated years of service and 30 per cent were added to our salary as a result of that. And that's why our salaries were always higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea of why in May of 1992 the TO would be paid so much more than the police?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to tender 1391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Hannis, what do you wish the Chamber to elicit from this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I may not be able to fully explain that to you until all the evidence is in. And in that case, perhaps I should mark it for identification. But I think the fact that this gross disproportionality after the war with this group, with this individual, may tie into explain why certain people were in certain positions, why certain crimes, we say, were covered up to protect certain individuals. I think this joint criminal enterprise as charged can be explained, in part, by some of the criminal conduct of people that we allege are members of it. If that's not enough for you now, then I ask that it be marked for identification, and I'll try to make a further tie-in and connection later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P327, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd like to next look at what has already been marked for identification as 1D67.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, this is a document dated, I think, the 4th of May, 1992, from the provisional government of Zvornik. Do you recognise the stamp on that document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This is the seal of the Executive Board of the Zvornik Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it's an order for payment of 10.000 dinars for the needs of the special unit volunteers from Loznica. The money to be taken over by Zuca. Were you aware in 1992 that Zuca was being paid by the government of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: They were paid by the Zvornik government, Zuco's unit was, and the MUP paid for another group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on what a occurred before, when I think the Defence showed this to witness ST-144, we had identification of the handwritten signature. I would now move to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the number it has now? Okay. It's 1D67 in evidence then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. A couple of more I would like to show you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you next 65 ter 2717. This relates to a couple of other groups you mentioned earlier in your testimony as having appeared in Zvornik who eventually, later, you said, joined the TO of the army. This is a conclusion by the temporary government regarding the level of compensation for members of the Territorial Defence for the month of May. It says the members will get 80.000 dinars. If you could look it at --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's English page 2, and I'm looking for paragraph 7. I think it is on the page for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 7, Mr. Panic. Do you see that last sentence there where it says "... the special task units under the command of Nisko and Pivarski all get 100.000 dinars." Do you you know what these special task units were assigned to do or were doing in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know about them when they joined the TO. And as for Lieutenant Vladan Martic, I know he was in the military police. And I know of Captain Miloje, he had some reconnaissance units that were stationed in Glinica. And as for Niski and Pivarski when they joined in, I don't know. For awhile they were independent, and then for some period of time they were with the army, but as for exactly when, I don't know. Now, judging by this document, they were paid by the interim government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in terms of where they were and what they were doing in Zvornik municipality, did you see or hear or otherwise get information about what they were doing? Were they just sitting around the Territorial Defence command office? Were they out in the field? You must have some knowledge or information about what they were doing that you can share with us.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: This unit of Pivarski spent most of its time in a town called Drinjaca in Zvornik municipality. I didn't go up there at the time during the war, but they were in Drinjaca most of the time. That's some 14 kilometres from Zvornik in the direction of Sarajevo. As for Niski, he was mostly in Scemlija, in Snagovo, in Karakaj, the suburb areas. Now, as to what he did there, I don't know. I know that he used to strip even some Serbs naked and force them to join the army in Celopek and Scemlija and some other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were aware that in late April, May, June, even in July that there were certain combat operations in the field in Zvornik municipality where Muslim villages were liberated, to use a word used by some, where they were asked to surrender their weapons and then the people were moved out, the men were detained, women and children were moved out of the municipality? That was going on, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And which forces or which units among all these we've been talking about were engaged in doing that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: In most of the cases all of them took part, especially Niski's group and Pivarski's group. They used to capture people and then set up prisons. And then later on there were court orders, at least that's how it should be, to the effect that these facilities were taken over by police, and security was from then on provided by police. And then from Bijeli Potok and Djulici some 5- or 6.000 women and children were moved out, and then about 700 men were detained in the technical school centre in Karakaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I follow-up on that question, could I tender 2717, the provisional government decision about the amount of payment for certain units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted as Exhibit P328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall and can you tell us some of the places where these detention facilities were being set up to take in the people that were being captured by Pivarski, Niski, and others?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: The prison was in Zvornik in the administrative building Novi Izvor and in the misdemeanour court. Then there was another prison facility in Ekonomija, and then also at Ciglana, the brickworks in Novi Izvor, and then later on there was one in the technical school centre in Karakaj. And as for Kozluk settlement, everybody was moved out of there via the Drina River and sent to Subotica. And then there was also a detention facility at the Dom in Celopek.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understood your answer, these detention facilities were initially set up by those that were making the arrest or making the captures and bringing these people in, but I understood from, I think, from your prior statement or prior testimony that eventually the police came to be asked or ordered to serve as guards at those facilities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them except for the technical school centre, which was held by a unit called Karakaj Company. As for Novi Izvor, Celopek, Ekonomija, all of that was taken over by police member. Now, whether this was done pursuant to a court order or pursuant to an order issued by their immediate superior, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Karakaj company at KTS, the technical school, what were they? Were they a police formation, a TO formation? To whom did they belong?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Initially before the Army of Republika Srpska was established, it was the TO of Karakaj. And later on there was a Karakaj company with the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You started to mention, or I think you referred to an earlier answer about the Bijeli Potok or Djulici. Can you tell us what that was or where that was?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: These are places, some call them Bijeli Potok, some call them Djulici. It's 7 kilometres from Karakaj in the direction of Sapna.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened there? Did you have some involvement in the activity that took place there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think it was the 1st of June when Commander Marinko Vasilic called me to come to his office and told me that the Crisis Staff had made arrangement with the politicians of the Muslim Zvornik for the citizens from Klisa and the surrounding places to go down to Bijeli Potok and that they were asking to be allowed to go to the Muslim territory. For that purpose, trucks were to be made at their disposal to take them from Kalesija. So he ordered me to select about 10 or 15 police officers, and he told me that my only task was to help them board these vehicles, whereas all the rest would be done by the army. They would take them out of Klisa, and the trucks were going to be waiting there and they will continue towards Memici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell the Judges what happened when you got there. What did you see? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: When I came to Bijeli Potok, there was a column of men on the asphalt road. At the head of the column was my colleague Agan Lupic, a fellow police officer who used to work with me before. On the left in a big field were a crowd of women, elderly men, and children. They were separated from the column of the men. And that every three or four metres a soldier was standing. When I arrived I greeted my colleague Dupic [as interpreted], and he asked me, Petko, which truck am I to board? And he said, Since we are going to Memici, shall I board the first truck? And I said yes. And the rest followed him. They climbed onto the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Agan Lupic was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Agan, yes, he was a Muslim policeman in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did anything unusual happen while the men were getting on to the trucks? Did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: After a while I heard shots coming from a bridge in Bijeli Potok. I went over there to see what was happening, but then one soldier told me that this was going on up there below the houses where we were securing the area, and don't go there. All we had to do, as I was told, was to assist with loading the people into the truck, so I went back. When I came to the trucks, one of the policemen told me that Dragan Spasojevic had come and took Agan Lupic from the truck and he drove him to Karakaj. I asked how did he do that, and he told me he put him in a car. The people were being loaded on to the trucks. And after that they started loading women, old people, and children who were on the left-hand side on this meadow. So by the evening, everybody was on board the trucks, and I returned to the hotel with my policemen and reported to commander Vasilic - and there was Niko Miljanovic there as well - that all the citizens of Klisa had left for Memici. About two or three hours later, I heard that 700 people remained behind in the technical school centre. One or two days later, I heard that the shots that we had heard in Bijeli Potok meant that the army had killed about five or six Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you because I didn't know any of those soldiers in this army, because one day beforehand, they had arrived from Brnjaca in Zivinice municipality, and they immediately took those houses, Muslim houses. Only in Belgrade during the court proceedings Marinko stated, who was the commander at the time, that he had gone to the TO staff in order to inquire why these men were kept and that somebody, he didn't say who, that they were kept there for exchange because in Tuzla there were 4.000 Serbs detained in a stadium waiting to be exchanged. But I only learned about that in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me clarify a few things that are aren't fully clear to me. What was the unit at Bijeli Potok that was there in control of the Muslims that were going to be put on buses and trucks? Who were they? Whose command were they under? Was this a VRS unit?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Already the VRS was established at that time, and there was a so-called Brnik company commanded by Captain Mijatovic or Mitrovic, I'm not sure about his surname. Then there was also the Petkovac company from Zvornik municipality; Grbavac company also; and on the spot there, on the right-hand side where the loading of people was taking place, I saw elements of the Celopek company who I think was commanded or led by a prominent member of the SDS party, Ostoja Ikonic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ostoja Ikonic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Agan who was taken away to Karakaj by Dragan Spasojevic, do you know what happened to him? Did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I heard that Dragan first took him to his house in Mali Zvornik, then in the evening he took him to the municipal building in Zvornik, and probably the Crisis Staff discussed with him whether he should go to Memici and Tuzla to negotiate the exchange, and that they drove him as far as Memici. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is he still alive, do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I heard that he is still alive, living in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened to the 700 or so men who were taken to Karakaj, to the technical school?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I ask -- may I ask, do we have an exact precise date on the events in Bijeli Potok?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't think we do. I haven't asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us approximately what date this occurred, when you went to Bijeli Potok?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: The 1st of June. The 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I think you told us it was during a time when Marinko Vasilic was commander?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the commander. And Milos was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us, if you know, what became of those 700 or so Muslim men who were taken to Karakaj Technical School?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Two or three days later, rumours started circulating around the town that there were killings being committed, that the paramilitary units, Zuco's men and Repic's men were killing people in the technical school centre. That they were taking them down to the slaughter-house where they were executing them in front of the slaughter-house. And I believe that the majority of those men was indeed killed there. Maybe a small number of them were transferred to the prison in Batkovici. So far as the killing sites or perhaps even burial sites are concerned, I don't know who decided this, whether it was the staff or hygiene and sanitation commission made up of a number of members, including Petar Tanic, a policemen who kept records of those either by name, if they had an ID, or just a John Doe if they didn't. And there was also Milan Radic who was a truck driver, and he was probably taking these bodies from the technical school centre in his truck to be buried somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you mentioned the slaughter-house, is that the one that's known as Gero's Slaughter-House or Gero's Slaughter-House?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a slaughter-house by the Drina River. I don't remember his name. He was called Gero, and had he this slaughter-house before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you -- in addition to hearing about these killings, did you have information about some killings of detained Muslims that happened at Celopek Dom?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Not directly. The reserve station in Celopek was run by Cvjetko Jovic [phoen], and he told me on more than one occasion that he couldn't stand it any longer there. Whenever Repic appeared with a black hat, a long rain coat, and a knife in his hand, which made all the guards move away, and that he was coming to the Dom in order to cut off people's parts of bodies, that he was killing them, taking money from them, and that they didn't dare confront him. I told him you should send a report to Commander Marinko. And I, myself, are going to -- am going to inform him as well. If you don't feel secure, just try to survive because Repic didn't care whether he was killing Serbs or Muslims. After that he was arrested either by a special unit or someone else because we couldn't do that. And also Zuca was arrested by a special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Some questions about that. Can you tell me approximately when this was that you had your first conversation with Cvjetko Jovic about Repic and what was happening at Celopek Dom?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not able to give you any date. It's been a long time ago. But I know that Miko Miljanovic drove those men away because Slavko -- and those were mostly people from Divic. They were supposed to be taken to Volovska Luka, and when he took them there, some remained there, whereas the others returned. Slavko asked Miko, because he was tired, to drive them to Celopek because that's what the commander had ordered him. Maybe Miljanovic would be able to give you a date. That's all I heard, and therefore I'm not able to give you any specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To help narrow down a possible date, you said that you told Cvjetko he should send a report to Commander Marinko. So it must have been during the time when Vasilic was serving as commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, commander. It was sometime in June. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, that is helpful. You said that the guards, when they saw Repic coming, they would -- they didn't dare confront him. Were these police or reserve police?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't catch the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of them were reserve police because active duty police were not trained in combat activities. Those were regular and ordinary policemen, and you cannot confront anyone who did so many atrocities or things that he did in Croatia and elsewhere; therefore, they didn't dare confront him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you said the people who were detained there were mostly from Divic. Do you know when the Muslim people from Divic had been captured and detained, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know at what time. But in the beginning they were detained in Divic at the playground where they were guarded by the Karakaj company. Now, when Slavko received an order to take them to Volovska Luka, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your job before the war, did you have occasion to know personally some of the people from Divic?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I knew most of the people in Divic, but I don't know who was detained. Some were detained even before the conflict broke out, and then they crossed over to Mali Zvornik. For example, I knew a man who everybody called "Francuz," meaning the Frenchmen, I know that he was detained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you told Cvjetko to report to Marinko Vasilic about what was happening in Celopek, and you said that you would inform him as well. Did that happen? First of all, do you know if Cvjetko reported; and secondly, did you tell Marinko?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that Cvjetko informed Marinko, and so did I. And I have a confirmation for that at the trial in Belgrade when Marinko denied knowing anything. However, when the judge read out to him Cvjetko's statement about his coming to the school for meeting, he says, Yes, I did come to -- for this meeting. And then the judge asked me, Now what do you think? And he said, I think he is telling the truth because he admitted coming to the meeting to this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall any details about when you personally informed him? Did that take place face to face, and what response, if any, did he make when you told him about it?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. That was 17 years ago. Whether anyone was with him or with me, I cannot remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to press you a little bit on that. You knew some of those people who were being detained there, and you had heard what sounds to me like pretty scarey information about what was happening with Repic. You don't recall what Marinko said when you told him about this?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I honestly don't remember. I think that he said something to the effect that he was going to inform someone and that some dispatch was written to that effect, but I'm not sure. I think he sent a dispatch to Bijeljina. Since we sent a dispatch on such trivial incidents such as chasing out Gogic, I'm sure that a dispatch describing such a major event would have gone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned Gogic, that takes me to the next thing I wanted to ask you about. You describe several of the formations that were in Zvornik. Who was Gogic and who were his men?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think his first name was Milorad Gogic. There were 11 or 12 members from Loznica, from Seselj's party. Initially when they came into Zvornik they were there, but then they left after awhile. And Milos Pantelic was appointed chief. They were brought again and were given police uniforms, and they were paid by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did they do in Zvornik after they got police uniforms and were being paid by the police? Were they doing any work?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: For the most part they were engaged in what we were supposed to do, which is man check-points or search the houses. And I know that on or about the 25th of May when Slavko Eric was killed, that they were with him in this combat in Kamenica. But, as I say, for the most part, they were around the town itself and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any alleged illegal or criminal conduct that they engaged in at the check-points?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: There were rumours that they were looting, that during searches they were seizing money and gold, but I didn't see that. On one occasion when a police officer, Boro Zekic, protested about what they were doing on the bridge at the check-point, they beat him up, although he was a police officer too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in an earlier answer that you kicked out Gogic's men, I take it you mean you, the regular police in Zvornik. Can you tell the Judges about when that happened and how that came about.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: That happened on the evening of the 27th of July. The regular police was coming back from the field, from the lines where we went because we were told that four members of the Sekovic company were captured. However, we didn't find any members of any unit; we only found a TV set and bicycle. So when we returned at the entrance to Zvornik, these Gogic's men stopped us and started searching us. We resented that, and, therefore, we went to the station and informed Marinko Vasilic that they were not supposed to do the police work, that they should, once they were brought here, be sent out to be deployed on the front line. Marinko then told us that we had to report to Kalesija municipality to hold the line there. I said I'm not going there. This is not my job. And he said, Then the police should go. And I said if I'm not going, neither is the police going to go, but you should rather send Gogic. He refused to do that, and about 30 or 40 of us policemen were annoyed, and, therefore, we agreed to capture the house where the Gogic's men were. We disarmed them, and we chased them across the Drina. We took over the bridge and everything else that they held. Marinko Vasilic didn't like that. He didn't want to go home, and we kept him there over the night. The next day he and Brano Grujic resigned from their positions. And one or two days later, a special unit arrived that had provided us previously with some tapes. They arrested all Zuco's men. And that is when Mico Lokanjcevic was brought from the MUP to be the chief and Brano Mihajlovic to be the commander. For a month I had been receiving some threats from Gogic's men that I better not go to Loznica and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll come back to those events in late July. Let me ask you one further question about outsiders who came to Zvornik and then were put in the police force. In addition to Gogic and his men, were you aware of a man from Teslic who had the nickname Crni?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Crni came with 12 or 13 men. They were originally from Teslic, and they used to be at the fronts in Croatia with Captain Dragan. According to the story that was circulating, Crni was one of the officers of Captain Dragan. As soon as they arrived, they gave them police uniforms, they received the same salary as we did, they were an independent group, regardless of the fact that they belonged to the police. They did what Crni told them to do, they searched the area, toured the area. They didn't bring anything to the MUP premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say they gave them police uniforms and they received the same salary. Who in Zvornik gave these guys police uniforms and paid them a salary from the police budget?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Since at the time MUP wasn't paying us properly either, that this was some kind of an agreement between the government and the chief that Zuca's men were to be paid by the municipality and that they were to be paid by MUP. I'm not a hundred per cent sure, but I think that that is how it was approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately when did they come? What month, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
