utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say. I don't know when the attack on Kula was. They came on that day in the evening, and they participated in the attack on Kula, which is above Zvornik, but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whom was the chief of the SJB at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think it was still Milos Pantelic. Because the late Slavko was still alive and Slavko was killed on the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So sometime before the 25th of May this happened?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you, in the MUP, both before and during the war, was there a general requirement for an SJB to send daily reports up to the regional services centre to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Before the war that was the regular procedure, to send a dispatch about any event of interest. Other than that there was a compiled report sent every evening. In the beginning of the war, communication lines were not functioning properly, but once they did become operational, reports were being sent. At the beginning of the war, we belonged to CSB in Bijeljina. And then if communications lines were down, then they used courier service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when did the lines become operational again? In your area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were fixed quickly within 15 or 20 days because there was no significant damage to them in Zvornik, and there wasn't any in Bijeljina. This is counting from the 6th, the day of the separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, next I'd like to show the witness a series of four documents that are all in the nature of daily reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, I'm not interested so much in the content of these documents. I just want to ask if you recognise the format and who has signed these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first one is 65 ter 2935.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name and the signature at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milos Pantelic, he was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if we can reduce and see the whole document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is dated the 3rd of June. It appears to be in the nature of a daily report for what happened the preceding day on 2 June. And just the first paragraph -- this is being sent to Security Services Centre in Bijeljina. But in the first paragraph -- in the first paragraph, the last portion you'll see it says "... which is to be forwarded to the Sarajevo CSB." Is that because you didn't have a connection to the Sarajevo like you did to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It's possible that initially we didn't have communication with them. In Bijeljina, how should I put it, when the first clashes broke out, there wasn't much damage caused, so the communication lines were established with Bijeljina faster, re-established.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that during this time in May, June, July of 1992, that there was some -- some confusion or conflict about which CSB Zvornik should be under? Whether it should be under Bijeljina or whether it should be under Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: At the beginning we were under Bijeljina, and then for a period of time, whether it was in August or when, we were placed under the Sarajevo Romanija centre, or whatever it was called. And then later on we were moved back under Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why that was happening?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. This is high politics. This is way above me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 2935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P329, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next if we can look at 65 ter 328.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, this is a similar document. Do you recognise the name and the signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milos Pantelic again, chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And again this appears to be a daily report; and, again, it's going to Bijeljina, but in the first paragraph it has the wording "... with the proviso that it be forwarded to Sarajevo CSB."

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: CSB Sarajevo, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down to see the stamp on the -- sorry, scroll up, I guess, to see the stamp on the -- not that stamp, but a different one, at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read that? My translation shows that being received in --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Bijeljina Sec -- I wouldn't be able to read the first word, and then it says, "Bijeljina Secretariat for ..." And then this is unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The translation I have indicates it's, received telegram number such and such.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Looks like "people's," "Secretariat for people's ..." I'm unable to read it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P330, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next one is 2936.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, another one, do you recognise the name and signature?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Can you enlarge it? Yes, Milos Pantelic again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again the same sort of daily report, this one dated the 5th of --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, to inform Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 2936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more in this series, if I may, and that would be 329. 65 ter 329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what is the purpose of tendering four variations of essentially the same document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't know if I should tender two or six. I selected four. One reason I selected four is because I have this series within the four or five days. And also you'll see in the upcoming documents that there's a change in the chief, so it helps us identify which date this gentleman ceased to be the chief and when someone else became the new chief. And also, you've heard, I think, that the Defence in this case is partly based on the fact that saying there was chaos, communications weren't working, et cetera, so I think it's important for the Prosecution to establish that fact. With your leave, if I may have one more. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This document, do you recognise this signature, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Again, chief of the station, Milos Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is dated the 8th of June for events occurring on the 7th, and again that proviso to forward it to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Again to be forwarded to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we tender that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P332, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at 65 ter number 2937.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, in a moment you'll see this is a document dated the 9th of June concerning a list of ammunition and weapons on stock at the police station and a request for additional ones. Dated the 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the bottom of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name and signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marinko Vasilic became chief here, and the date is 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: July or June?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: June, June. 9th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 2937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P333, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on what we've just seen, Mr. Panic, it appears that Vasilic became the new chief sometime on the night of the 8th or the morning of the 9th. Do you know how that happened?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: On the 7th or 8th or 9th, around there. I heard that Milos was leaving due to health reasons. He was leaving service and going back to Loznica, back home. Now, whether there was -- that was true, whether there were some additional reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who selected or appointed Marinko Vasilic to the post of chief? Was that done within the MUP, was it done by the Crisis Staff or the temporary government? What do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Earlier according to the rules, there should have been a proposal from the station and then MUP should have approved it. But I don't know whether at that time it was already the MUP passing the decisions, or whether the Crisis Staff was still appointing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we next see 2938.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see the name and signature on this one? You recognise it?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marinko Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this appears to be a cover letter for the last document we looked at which was a list of materiel and equipment in the SJB.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Such a request for that kind of equipment, weapons, ammunition, et cetera, is this where a police station chief would send his request, to the CSB?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible. It's possible that they had additional members of the reserve forces join them, so they were lacking weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is, is this the appropriate unit to which to send such a request from the police station, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: The CSB was above the SJB, unless they were reporting to MUP because here they say that this needs to be forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior. If they had no communication links with MUP, then they would send it to CSB, and then CSB would forward it to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender 2938.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. And, Mr. Hannis, this is the point -- time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P334, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I have one request. One of the exhibits I want to show the witness is a lengthy document, and I wonder if I could hand him a copy of the B/C/S so he could look at it during the break. It might speed things when I show it to him later on. If the Defence has no objections. It's the annual report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the next document I would like to you to take a look at is 65 ter 2939. This is dated the 25th of June, 1992, regarding a request for equipment, and if we could look first at the bottom of the page. Do you recognise the name and the signature on this one?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marinko Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we'll see this request is addressed at the top of the page to, what my English translation says is the republican TO or Territorial Defence of Serbia and Belgrade requesting certain equipment. Were you aware that your chief had sent a request for such equipment to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that he had sent the request, but I did hear that the equipment came from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in the first sentence it mentions that the Zvornik public station has an active and reserve component currently numbering about 500 members. Is that consistent with your knowledge of how many policemen you had around the end of June 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there were that many. Perhaps 350. I don't know that there were 500. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Does your estimate include Crni and his men, and Gogic and his men?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just referring to policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to equipment that you, regular policemen in Zvornik, had, what kind of uniforms and weapons did you have in April, May, June, July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: We had multi-coloured camouflage uniforms in olive drab [indiscernible], and police uniforms. So as far as the equipment goes, we were equipped.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Mostly automatic and semi-automatic rifles, and an occasional machine-gun, 7.62. And later on, we had some 84 ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 2939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P335, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next if I could show you 65 ter number 313.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This next document, Witness, relates to an issue we talked about regarding which CSB Zvornik was supposed to be under or report to. You see the name Mico Stanisic and a signature, although it appears to be, I can't tell if that's --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, minister of the interior. But it's almost like somebody signed for him. Mico Stanisic is typed, and then it says "for."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, that was my question. Is that a "za" written there before the signature?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think so, somebody signed for him. He could authorise a person to sign for him, for the minister, and the same could be done for commander, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could see the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first paragraph seems to indicate this is a response to something that had been sent from Zvornik, and this document is informing that Zvornik belongs to Sarajevo CSB. It's dated the 16th of August. Did you see this document back then, or were you aware of its contents?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't see the document, but when it arrived, whether it was a meeting of the leaders, a meeting of the police, the information was given that from that point on we belong to the centre of the Sarajevo Romanija region, or whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who conveyed that information to you at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but most likely the commander called up senior workers, head of communications and so on, and then it was well known to whom the information was distributed on afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I move to tender 313.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P336, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next could we show the witness 65 ter 2940. 2940.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, this is dated 29 June 1992, has the typed name Mico Stanisic and a signature. On the left at the bottom, there's a handwritten note that's been translated for me as "received" and then the name "Laza Dragicevic." Do you know a person by that name?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, we didn't have anybody under the name of Laza Dragicevic. Head of communications was Vukasin Danojlovic. I don't know who Laza Dragicevic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This communication is directing Zvornik public security to allow Kalesija SJB to use a temporarily confiscated Golf vehicle which had been with that police station before. Were you aware of this, or did you hear anything about this in late June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know which vehicle this refers to. There was some talk that there was a Golf in Kalesija in Osmace that was confiscated and that Zuca's group confiscated a vehicle that belonged to Velibor Ostojic. But I'm not sure what this is about. And as far as I know, in Osmace, there were people with the last name Dragicevic. And at that time Osmace belonged to the Zvornik station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us where Kalesija SJB was?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Kalesija is halfway between Zvornik and Tuzla, and that was under the Muslim command, that was in the Muslim Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that true throughout the entire 1992, that Kalesija was within the Muslim territory?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, only I heard that Zuco's units entered Kalesija, but it did belong to the Muslim Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any other questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May that be marked for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P337, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to show you, Witness, 65 ter number 309. Witness, this is dated the 17th of June, 1992, and it purports to be a report about an inspection conducted at Zvornik SJB, and partially about the situation in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The names are on the last page, and if we could take a quick look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see the typed name Dragan Andan and Danilo Vukovic, those are inspectors. Did you know Dragan Andan?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think I saw him once or twice. I think on one occasion it was before the specials came in and expelled Zuco's men. And the second time, I don't remember when I saw him. As for this person Vukovic, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that these two men had come to do an inspection of the Zvornik police station in late May or early June 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't because at that time, at the beginning of war, many inspectors from the former MUP came to us and they were refugees from Sarajevo and Zenica. They came and started working for all the criminal investigation service. Then they would be there for a day or two and then they would go on to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did your chief at the time make you aware of the results of any inspection that had been carried out by inspectors who came for that purpose during May or June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't recall. I really don't remember. We may have talked about it, but then again maybe I wasn't there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to page 4 of the B/C/S, and it's the bottom -- it begins at the bottom of page 4 of the English. I will direct your attention to a couple of things that these inspectors wrote about, and ask you what you might know about that. For you, it begins the top of your page. And in the English: "Besides the war activities in which the employees of Zvornik police station participate directly, in order for patrol service to function in Zvornik, it's necessary to withdraw police employees from securing premises on the territory of Zvornik ..." And then it goes on down, skipping a sentence: "The officials at SJB Zvornik have tried to find a solution through the government. In other words, they suggested that the TO members secure these premises and police return to their daily activities. However, they were not met with understanding." Did that happen? Are you aware of that kind of discussion about, We need to take the police away from guarding these facilities and let them get back to regular police work? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't present when that was discussed, but I knew about that because even before that period, we would discuss this issue at the station in the way of that these facilities should be given either to the police or the army because there were clashes between the police and the armies about whose jurisdiction it was. Therefore, we thought that the police should be sent back to town to do their regular work on maintaining law and order, and crime detection, et cetera. If necessary, then the brigade could call us to join combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we could go to the next page in the English. For you, Witness, it's the very next paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The inspectors indicated that: "SJB Zvornik comes across numerous problems regarding the activities by paramilitary formations." Besides the fact that the government of Zvornik municipality has through its decision banned the establishment of a training camp run by Captain Dragan, military authorities have allowed that the same be formed in the area of Divici. According to the senior staff at the SJB Zvornik, the same have also usurped the premises of Vidakovac motel and have gathered there a large number of persons criminally inclined. Were you aware of that? Is that consistent with what you saw and knew was going on in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Captain Dragan arrived sometime after the death of Slavko Eric on the 25th of May in Kamenica. They were killed there, and we couldn't pull out their bodies. Therefore, he offered to assist us in that. However, he never went to Kamenica, and two or three days later with the approval of the army, he occupied Vidakovac motel with his unit in which Crni was also there, and the two of them, the so-called Knindze, were before that in Croatia. And most of those who joined them were criminals who searched houses and stole property. The access to this facility had such high security level that is comparable to the one that is provided for a president of the state. No one was allowed to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me read you the last sentence in that paragraph. It says: "Due to such a decision and legalisation of the stay by criminally inclined persons in this area, the chief of SJB Zvornik, dissatisfied with the decision by military authorities, has submitted a request to be released from this duty." Who was the chief in Zvornik around the time this was happening? Was that Pantelic or Vasilic that this would be referring to? If you know.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that Pantelic was still in that position. Maybe that also impacted his decision to resign due to health reasons having seen that he was unable to do anything about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the timing seems to be consistent because this inspection appears to have occurred between May 29th and June 12th, and we saw earlier that Pantelic was last the chief on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: On the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 309.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] There appears to be no objection. Yes, it will be marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P338, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next if we could look at 65 ter 347, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, when we rise for the day at 1.45, you would have occupied the full four hours which constitutes a day's sitting, which is the time that you estimated you would use. Do we correctly anticipate that you would have completed your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to double-check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: By then at latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think I will be. But I would indicate, I did check with the legal officer when we started this session and -- because we had some preliminary matters, and we had a little longer break at one time, I was advised that I had used 2 hours and 12 minutes when we started. If I used 1 hour and 15 minutes now, to the end of this session, I estimate I'll have about 20 minutes left tomorrow, and I hope that I will finish within that 20, 25 minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next is 65 ter 347. This is dated the 23rd of July, 1992, Witness, and if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and just look at the name at the bottom of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You'll recognise that name we saw before, Dragan, Andan?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Andan Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is talking about the security situation in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we go to page 1 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Andan lists four groups that you had described for us earlier, Zuco, Pivarski, Niski, and Simo Chetnik. And you'll see he indicates as of this date, the approximate areas where these groups were located, Pivarski in Drinjaca, Niski in Kiseljak, Simo Chetnik in Malesic. Is that consistent with your information?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I also say that Simo was in Malesic, Pivarski in Drinjaca, and I didn't know the whereabouts of Niski.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 347.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P339, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next 65 ter 312.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Earlier today, Witness, you told us about a time came when you and regular members of the police decided to take action against one of these outsider groups. And in particular that was Gogic and his men. I think you told us that happened on or about the 27th of July. Do you recognise the document that is on the screen now, and if so, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I can't see clearly whether it's the minister of the interior from Pale. This is a letter describing the event, and it was signed by Momcilo Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it makes reference -- it makes reference to a group of people from Loznica who --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Gogic's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- were prone to committing crimes, and that they had been removed and --

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: On the 27th of July at around 2300 hours. We chased them out into Mali Zvornik without their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it appears that you, the police in Zvornik, are requesting some urgent assistance from the Presidency or the Ministry of the Interior; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that same evening, we sent to the Bijeljina centre two of our men to inform them about what we had done, that was Miko Miljanovic and Milan Micic. And those people at the centre were not very satisfied because we did that, since they had planned to use their own resources and chase out all those paramilitary groups including Zuco's one. And we told them that we should -- they told us that we should be really careful not to let Zuco escape because we would be blamed. And then the next day they came and arrested Zuco's unit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your men who went to Bijeljina to inform about what had happened with Gogic's men, are they the ones who came back and told you that there was a plan in Bijeljina to come down and do something about Zuco and the others?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They said that they had already planned to capture the paramilitary units, but they didn't know anything about this plan, and we were just ahead of them and they only just warned us to be careful not to allow Zuco to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they send you any kind of equipment or anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, not then, but during the evening they brought us some ribbons to tie around our upper arms in order to recognise our group. We were in the hotel at the time and we needed these ribbons for recognition purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To identify you as not being part of Zuco's or the others who were intended to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, Zuco's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you personally take any part in that operation to arrest the Yellow Wasps and the others?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, we were told to go on with our usual business, to stay in the hotel, and they would do all the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, who actually, then, arrested the paramilitary groups? Was it the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the Special Police of Mr. Karisik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge were there also any federal police from the federal MUP in Serbia led by Mico Davidovic that took part in the operation?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. As I told you, we were told to stay put in the hotel. They arrested them, took them away to Bijeljina, and I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And similarly, do you know whether or not any military police or military security administration personnel participated in the round-up?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't see, but I think there was no one else apart from this special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how many men came down with that special unit to participate in the arrest, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell because they were not in one place. They had their own plan, one group was surrounding or jumping across the fence near the hotel, the others were running through the parks, we really didn't know how they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Shortly after that event on the 29th of July, did you have a change of chief in the police department?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you a document. This is 65 ter number 335.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I guess before we go to that, Your Honours, I would like to tender 312.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted, marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P340.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, the next document I want to show you is dated the 2nd of August, 1992. Do you see the names at the bottom of that document?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You recognise them?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. Marinko Vasilic, the chief until that point; replaced by Lokanjcevic Milorad, and Branislav Mihajlovic, became commander; and Ratko Jovicic was the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters are asking if you could repeat the last two positions. They didn't quite hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: From -- starting from Ratko Jovicic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps if he repeats the whole answer, it would be simpler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recognise all these names. Marinko Vasilic, former chief. Milorad Lokanjcevic, replaced Vasilic in the position of chief. Branislav Mihajlovic came and was appointed commander. Ratko Jovicic was chief of the CID, of criminal investigation department. And Cvijetin [phoen] Lekic was a traffic inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know where Marinko Vasilic went after he was relieved of his position? What became of him?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: He went to the municipality, he was there on stand by for a period of time. And later he got employed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the last word. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry, the interpreters didn't hear the last word about where or how he got employed.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Oh. He was -- he became employed with the customs office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- oh, one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did Lokanjcevic come from?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milorad, aka, Mico Lokanjcevic, was from the village Brodac, Bijeljina municipality. Before he used to work as the chief of police station in Kalesija, that was before the war. He is now retired and lives in the village of Brodac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who chose him and appointed him for that position as the new chief in Zvornik? Was that the Crisis Staff, or was that the MUP? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that already then, because he came after the dismissal of Vasilic. He and Branislav Mihajlovic came from the security centre of Bijeljina. They were appointed by ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry. It's translated, "They were appointed by ..." And then we don't hear your answer. By whom or what?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: By the centre -- security centre of Bijeljina, public security centre of Bijeljina and the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender 335.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, next I want to ask you a little bit about some of the Muslim detainees. Is it correct that even in late August after there had been some international furor about Manjaca and Omarska, there were still Muslim civilians that were detained in the Zvornik area. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date when the prisons in Zvornik were closed and moved to Batkovic. It is possible, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 1585.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll tell you as it's coming up on the screen, this is dated the 29th of August, 1992. And it's from Commander Colonel Dragutin Ilic from the Eastern Bosnia Corps. I think you've told me before, you recognised his name as a member of the VRS; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I have never -- Dragutin Ilic. He was writing to the Zvornik Brigade. He is probably from the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that's correct. You see his message is to the Zvornik Brigade: "Hand over the Muslims you have in the Divic centre, 78 people, to the Zvornik SJB. They are civilians, so they are in their jurisdiction, not in that of a military unit." First of all, can you tell us where the Divic centre was in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: The Divic centre, I explained, it's a village above Zvornik where Radikovac was. But I think that at the time there were no Muslim detainees in Divic, but that from the Dom in Celopek, certain prisoners were returned to the prison called Novi Izvor and misdemeanour court in Zvornik. That situation remained until 1993 when I saw a document about 13 Muslims who were sent purportedly to log woods or trees on Crni Vrh, that was in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know anything about 78 civilians being transferred from the army to the Zvornik SJB around the end of August?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I don't. But as I've said, it's possible that those who were detained in Novi Izvor and at the municipal court, that it was them. They had nothing to do with them. Twelve or thirteen people from there were allegedly taken to Crni Vrh to cut timber there allegedly, and then they were killed, people from Divic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That event you are just describing, can you tell us when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I saw in one document either here or in Tuzla indicating that that was in January. From the prison in the misdemeanour court, they were to take out 13 prisoners and they were to be dressed in the police uniforms, the winter ones, and that they were to be taken to Crni Vrh to cut timber there. The uniforms were put on them, and as was stated at the court in Tuzla by Sredoje Vukojevic who was the prison warden, that in -- Mico Lokanjcevic conducted the inspection, and a military truck arrived, 150 type, and these people were boarded on the truck and allegedly taken to Crni Vrh to cut timber, but they never returned. And in the evening on the radio, it was reported that a Muslim terrorist group numbering 13 people appeared in Crni Vrh and were successfully liquidated by the Army of Republika Srpska. And it was then that they started believing that it was these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to have 1585 marked for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P342 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the witness is saying January for this event. I suppose that January --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I think that's unrelated [realtime transcript read in error "related"] to these 78 people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to show you 65 ter 3025. Witness, this is a list of names, purportedly police who were working at the prison in August of 1992. And do you recognise the men named there, that list of ten?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were they policemen in the Zvornik SJB at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we can go to the signature on the bottom right. It's the station commander. I guess it's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you recognise what is written there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I cannot, but MM could be Momcilo Maric, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I need to look at the next page in the B/C/S, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was Vojin Vukovic who became commander later. And this signature is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But is that Vukovic's signature?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. As for the policemen, seven of them have been sentenced to ten or so years in Sarajevo for these war events.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what specific war events? Related to the prison where they were guarding?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: For prisons. For prisons. Sretena [phoen] was given ten years; the others, seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to tender 3025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P343, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Panic, just to clarify so there's no confusion, the Vojin Vukovic who was commander in August 1992 is not the same person that is known by the nickname Zuco, that's Vojin Vuckovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. One is Vuckovic, one is Vukovic. And Vojin Vukovic used to work for the Ministry of the Interior before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And speaking of Vuckovic, Zuco, were you aware that after he was arrested in late July in Zvornik, he was detained for a month and then released at the end of August when no charges were filed at that time? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I heard that they had been released from prison. Now, as to what was done, whether any reports were made, I don't know. This was most likely done by the Prosecutor in Bijeljina since they were detained there and I don't know what ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Goran Zugic who worked in the police station?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came from Tuzla, and he worked for the state security in Tuzla, and then he came to the state security in our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an exhibit that's 65 ter number 298.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document dated the 5th of September, 1992. And it appears to be some information from Goran Zugic, although the signature I believe is a signature for him. I think it's "za," z-a.

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Goran Zugic is typewritten and the rest "for ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I would indicate that at the top of the page it does talk about Zuco having been released after his arrest. And the report is talking about information they have about Vuckovic talking about maybe getting some of his men back together and settling accounts with MUP. And the next to the last paragraph says: "Bearing in mind the above, we and the Zvornik SJB have taken steps to observe the movements of Zuco's paramilitaries." Were you aware, or did you participate in any way in surveilling Zuco or his paramilitaries after he had been released at the end of August?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know when he was released. Most likely it was done by the state security since it was Goran Zugic who wrote this. At that time his wife was from the Celopek village, so most likely they had followed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender 298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P344, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that, Witness, I'd like to show you 65 ter number 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There's no signature on this document. It's dated the 10th of September 1992 in Pale. Purportedly from the National Security Service of the Republika Srpska. And it appears to be passing on that information that was in Mr. Zugic's report in a condensed fashion, delivered to the interior minister in the security organ of the army. You've not seen this document before; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two things in here I'll ask you about. One is it talks about Zuco trying to finish business in the region and suggests that he might try to launch an artillery attack on the Zvornik police station. Did you ever hear any talk or rumours about that?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that, but we did know that at the beginning, at the factory in Birac, he had started constructing an armoured train, but he didn't succeed in completing it. His work was banned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear the witness, his microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is mine. Okay, now mine is back on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, we had a technical malfunction, and I don't think the interpreters could hear all your answer, but I think you answered enough and started to talk about the armoured train. One other thing that says it that Zuco's return is mostly delayed by the presence of the special MUP unit in Zvornik. Was Milenko [realtime transcript read in error "Marinko"] Karisik's special unit still in Zvornik as of about the 10th of September, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Milenko, not Marinko Karisik. Milenko Karisik. It wasn't there the entire time. It wasn't there non-stop, but they used to come often at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender number 300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P345, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, we talked earlier about daily reporting from the SJB. In addition to those daily reports, did police stations and police chiefs also submit quarterly reports about the activities of their respective police stations, both before the war and after the war? Was that one of the standard requirements, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Yes, before the war especially. At the beginning of the war perhaps reports were not sent out immediately, but later on they sent quarterly reports as well. Especially once Mico Lokanjcevic came to his post, that became more regular, and there were no longer war activities in Zvornik and one was able to work properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter number 332. And, Your Honours, I would indicate in e-court it appears that we have no English translation of the first B/C/S page, but it's very brief. I'll just ask the witness if he can read the B/C/S that's on his screen right at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, can you read what is on the screen in front of you, what that document is or is entitled?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: "Report on ..." Then there's a portion that is unclear. Then it says, "SJB Zvornik from the 1st of April until the 30th of June 1992." And as for the unclear bit ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go then to the last page in both the B/C/S and English, I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name and the signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Marinko Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now if we could go back to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, we see that this is dated the 29th of June and purports to be sent to the Bijeljina CSB. Not Sarajevo, but to Bijeljina. And it's a report on the activities of the Zvornik police station between 1 April and 30 June. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document, but most likely this was sent to Bijeljina. And at that time we still belonged to the Bijeljina centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of that B/C/S page and at the top of page 2 in the English, Witness, you'll see under the heading "Task and duties of the National Security Service," the second paragraph says: "During this period 300 individuals were interviewed and 200 statements taken about activities of Muslim and other extremist groups and individuals." During that time-period between April and the end of June 1992, where was the security -- the National Security Service conducting interviews, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with this. People who were taken in, be it by the army or by the police, and sometimes even by the paramilitaries, would be taken to the state security and to the criminal investigations police department, and they were the ones who conducted interviews and wrote reports on what they had learned based from interviews. They would send it to the chief of the centre, chief of the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us physically where they were located during this time-period? Were they at Alhos, or were they somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: Later on the hotel and the SUP building were already operational in May and June. We used to work for awhile at the SUP building and continued living at the hotel. The crime investigations police had their premises on the second floor, and the state security on the fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During the time that you were based in Alhos, were you aware of any detained Muslims being interviewed there?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It's possible, but I didn't see that. It's possible. I saw that there were people who had been taken in and there were offices there. That was a large textile manufacturing company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you personally aware of any detained Muslims being beaten and/or killed during interviews or during detention in any of those facilities in the Karakaj area during 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I know of Standard. I came from the field one day and I know that three Muslims were killed on the ground floor of Standard. And in talking to people, I learned that he was killed by a member of the Milic company of the VRS. And why? Because allegedly a soldier from the Milic company had been killed near a monument, and they came, they found those three men there, and shot them right away in the hallway, Kara [as interpreted] Osmanovic or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when that was, since you said it was a VRS unit, I take it, it was after mid-May. Can you give us any more precise date or month?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: No, I can't. Perhaps it was late May while the Milic company was at Standard. I know that Nijazkara [phoen] Osmanovic was killed, Ilijas, and I don't know the third person's name, but he was also from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you or anybody else in the police report about this to the military police or military authorities so they might take appropriate action against the killers?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I think that since the military police were stationed there at the Standard building and that they were possibly present when it was actually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of the B/C/S and page 4 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, on your page there's a heading called "Task and Activities of the Police Station" and it's the second paragraph under there. It says: "As of 25 June 1992, 200 members of the reserve force were placed under the direct command of the Zvornik Municipality Brigade staff." Did you know about that, that 200 reserve police had been placed under command of the brigade staff?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that there were as many as 200, but I knew that a large number of men were taken off the reserve forces of police and transferred to the brigade. In Zvornik and in the surrounding towns, there was no combat activities in order to reduce the number of policemen who were conducting those duties. And I think that the brigade had sent a dispatching asking that the extra men be sent to them so that they could become members of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how it was decided or who decided that those reserve police would be given or loaned or placed under the command of Zvornik Brigade? Who in the police would have had the authority to make that kind of decision?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It depends on the period of time. It could have been decided by the chief himself, or he could have said to the commander, Make a selection of men who are no longer fit to serve and police, be it because of their attitude or something else, and send them to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next paragraph says: "In this period, the Zvornik police station employees participated in 15 combat operations, mopping up operations, and terrain searches." Did you, yourself, participate in any combat or mopping up operations?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: From the 25th of June, I don't know, it's possible. If I did go, then I went to Bandjerka. Most of the time I went with a company to the trenches in Bandjerka which is in Sekovic municipality. We would spend 15 days there and then come back. But I'm not certain that I took part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, for you, still on the same page. If you'll go down of five paragraphs to the one that begins with the number 336, "inspection outings." Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the top of the page in English, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question relates to the end of that paragraph, and it talked about police providing escort. It says: "... escort was provided for 30 columns of people and vehicles, a column of UNPROFOR, humanitarian aid, and persons escorted." My question is about persons escorted, were those Muslims who were moving out or being moved out of Zvornik municipality that were escorted by the police, if you know?

utterances.speaker: PETKO PANIC
utterances.text: It's possible that there were Muslims too. But this was already the 25th of June so I think that that was already the end, so there weren't many left. Could have been something else. Where it says here, people who require security, here they are referring to dignitaries. For example, a minister would come by, minister of Serbia, and he would require escort to Pale. Or a minister from Pale would come by, and he would require escort and security detail up to the border with Serbia. So it's mostly referring to them, people who require security detail. Because there used to be UNPROFOR there then and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender 332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P346, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think we are at 2 minutes from the end of the -- I have two small questions about the transcript if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Page 7, row 16, it said the assistant commander "Eric Slavko," and I wonder if that is Eric Slavko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I belive the first name ins Slavko, and the last name Eric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The last name is Eric. Is that the person that is killed on the 25th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eric, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Slavko is the first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So that should be corrected. And then on page 69, row 5, the events of January 1993. In the transcript it says that you said that's related to the 78 people. And I remember hearing you say that is not related; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's what I meant to say. I meant to say not related, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not related. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, may we break now, Your Honour. I would indicate I only have two more documents to ask about, a quarterly report and the annual report. And I will try to do that in 25 minutes tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we are not quite finished with your testimony yet, as you would have gathered, and we will resume in this courtroom at 9.00 tomorrow morning. So you having been sworn as a witness, you cannot speak to the lawyers from either side. And in your conversations with anybody outside of the courtroom, you can't discuss your testimony. And before we rise, I wish to extend the thanks of the Chamber to Mr. Khan whose assistance as duty counsel has enabled us to continue with a minimum of inconvenience and disruption in the peculiar circumstances we had. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
